newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian court to decide on alleged spy's health.
newsitem.headline: Russian court to decide on alleged spy's health.

text.p: Russia's counter-intelligence service said on Wednesday it had finished investigating the case of a Russian diplomat alleged to have spied for Britain and a court would now decide whether he had been sane at the time.

Platon Obukhov, 28, a second secretary in the Foreign Ministry's prestigious North America Department who wrote spy thrillers on the side, has been in prison awaiting trial on espionage charges since last April.
Obukhov's lawyers and parents say he is mentally unstable and unfit to stand trial. They say he has been ill since childhood and should be freed from prison and sent to hospital.

"A lawyer for the accused is now studying the evidence. After he has finished, the case will be passed to the court," a spokesman for Federal Security Service (FSB) told Reuters. "The court will decide on his mental problems and on whether to hospitalise him or to imprison him."
It was not clear when the case would be heard.

Soon after Obukhov's arrest several members of the British embassy in Moscow were expelled, accused of links to a Russian citizen who had access to classified information. In a Cold War-style tit-for-tat response Britain expelled some Russian embassy officials.
The FSB, a KGB successor which is responsible for domestic security, says Obukhov was sane while spying and that his illness now cannot free him from the legal process.

"He underwent psychiatric tests in 1996 and 1997 and his illness has been confirmed. But our point, which the doctors confirmed, is that he was not insane while committing his crimes," the spokesman said.

Platon Obukhov, the son of a former Soviet deputy foreign minister and top disarmament negotiator, said he had acted in "panicky fear". It was not clear how much classified information he had access to.

Several publications in the media compared him to the "giants of espionage", saying he had been in personal contact with British agents in Moscow. His parents said he did not have acess to classified information.
FSB chief Nikolai Kovalyov said recently foreign intelligence services were very active in Russia and that he was shocked by how cheaply many Russians were prepared to sell out their country.
He also claimed great success for an FSB telephone hotline, set up last month to invite Russians spying for foreign powers to turn themselves in to the FSB and become double agents.

Authorities have made much of the sentencing of two Russians, convicted separately of spying for Britain and the United States. FSB officials have said they caught 27 professional foreign spies last year and 60 Russians in the pay of foreign powers.
